title: Integration Architect Tactical Microcards v1
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, technical-first collection of microcards to help field sellers and solutions engineers quickly engage integration architects and platform teams during discovery and early technical scoping. These notes are intentionally short, quote-ready, and focused on the intersection of non-functional requirements (latency, throughput, isolation) and deployment options (hosted, dedicated, private).

When to use:
- Pre-demo qualification call with platform engineers
- Technical discovery threads in Slack/Email where you need a 2-3 minute rebuttal or a config suggestion
- Hand-off to SE for a rapid spike or POC

Audience:
- Integration Architects (primary): cares about network topology, dependency surface, and deployment automation
- Platform Engineers (secondary): cares about autoscaling, capacity planning, and SRE runbooks
- Product Engineers / PMs (context): cares about cost per call and UX latency budgets

Top-of-card layout (every microcard follows this):
- Problem statement (1 line)
- Quick fact (1 line)
- Script (30–90s) for seller/SE
- Actionable next step (one artifact or checkpoint)

Microcard A — Predictable throughput for real-time UI
- Problem statement: UI latency spikes under bursty traffic cause request timeouts and bad UX.
- Quick fact: Redwood Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools + burst capacity to keep p95 within booked SLOs.
- Script: "If you have a UX window that needs 100–200ms p95 for interactive features, we can reserve a dedicated pool sized for your steady traffic and configure burst capacity for traffic spikes. That means predictable tails and no surprise throttling during launches."
- Next step: Ask for per-minute qps distribution for a weekday peak and add it to the shared capacity spreadsheet (link below).

Microcard B — Data isolation & compliance question
- Problem statement: Security team insists on data never leaving a VPC and needs key control.
- Quick fact: Redwood Private supports customer KMS + audit logs and optional air-gapped on-prem package.
- Script: "We can run the inference control plane in your VPC, integrate with your KMS for keys, and enable audit trails for every request. For the most regulated customers we also offer an on-prem package that never egresses model inputs."
- Next step: Collect SOC/ISO/PCI specific requirements and route to the Private deployment checklist.

Microcard C — Cost control on chat-heavy workloads
- Problem statement: High token volumes from long context windows inflate monthly bills.
- Quick fact: Intelligent KV-prefix caching and batching can reduce token compute costs by 20–60% depending on repetition and prompt patterns.
- Script: "A quick audit of 1k representative sessions will surface repeat patterns to cache. We typically see 30% unit-cost savings after enabling prefix cache + adaptive batching for chat workloads."
- Next step: Request anonymized sample transcripts (remove PII) or a synthetic workload to estimate savings.

Microcard D — Fallback and graceful degradation for outages
- Problem statement: Need a plan when primary model or region is unavailable.
- Quick fact: Redwood routing policies allow automated fallback to smaller/cheaper variants and cross-region failover.
- Script: "We can configure an active fallback chain: primary high-capacity model -> quantized cheaper variant -> remote region, with metrics to monitor quality drift. That keeps your app responsive while preserving experience during incidents."
- Next step: Define acceptable fallback tiers (latency/quality tradeoff) and a canary policy for validation.

Common objections + short rebuttals (snippets to memorize)
- "We can't risk vendor lock-in": Redwood exposes model versioning and a standard API; customers can bring their models to Private deployments for full control.
- "Too expensive at scale": Show unit economics with batching and cache enabled; propose Dedicated reserved pricing vs hosted list pricing.
- "Latency can't be guaranteed": Highlight dedicated reservations, colocated regions, and kernel-level optimizations our serving runtime uses. Offer a short spike POC to demonstrate p95 improvements.
- "How do we measure quality impact of quantization?": We provide diff-eval harnesses tied to your prompt set so you can gate quantization with objective metrics.

Quick role-specific call scripts
- For an Integration Architect (tech-first, 90s): "We typically start by mapping ingress topology and expected peak qps. If you can share a small load profile and one representative prompt, we can recommend a model variant and capacity plan. From there we set up a 48 hour dedicated spike to validate p95 and per-token cost with your real traffic patterns."
- For a Platform Lead (ops-focused, 60s): "We offer reserved capacity and autoscaling policies that integrate with your SRE runbooks. We'll share a rollout playbook with canary steps, rollback criteria, and smoke tests so this fits into your current release cadence."
- For an Engineering Manager (exec+impact, 45s): "Expect a ~20–40% reduction in inference unit cost for chat flows after enabling caching and batching; we can commit to a spike to prove the numbers in your environment."

Demo & POC checklist for quick handoffs (copyable)
- Pre-demo: confirm sample prompts (1–3), target latency p95, expected peak qps, and which environment (hosted/dedicated/private).
- Provisioning: allocate trial API keys and optional dedicated pool for a 48–72 hour spike.
- Validation: synthetic load runner, p95 and cold-start histogram, token-cost estimate, and a diff-eval on deliverables.
- Handoff: Create a follow-up ticket with SLI/SLO targets and rollback steps.

Example customer scenario (retail search assistant)
- Context: Product team expects 10k daily active users with search bursts during promotions. Primary concerns are latency, relevance regression, and cost.
- Rapid plan: reserve dedicated pool sized for 500 qps steady, enable prefix caching for repeated query scaffolds, use a quantized reranker for initial pass and a higher-fidelity generator for rare, complex queries.
- Outcome objectives: p95 < 200ms, monthly inference cost < $X per DAU (placeholder to be updated after sample run), <1% relevance regression vs baseline.

Handoff & escalation notes for SEs
- If security asks for encryption-at-rest details, route to Private team doc CONFLUENCE-PRIV-22 (linked artifact).
- If SRE requests SLA wording, escalate to GTM legal via JIRA-GTM-451.
- If quantization effects are suspect, request a diff-eval with the Research team and tag research@redwood-inference.

Slide-outline for a 6-slide micro-deck (fast internal deck for sales)
1) Title & hook (customer problem + 1-line solution)
2) Architecture options (hosted / dedicated / private) with one-liner tradeoffs
3) Performance proof points (p95, throughput examples)
4) Cost levers (batching, cache, reserved capacity) with before/after example
5) POC plan & timeline (48–72h spike)
6) Next steps & decision checklist (data, qps, SLOs)

Playbook snippets to paste into Slack or email
- "Quick ask: can you share a 24h qps histogram and 10 representative prompts? We'll return a config and cost delta within 48 hours."
- "We recommend a 72h dedicated spike at X1 capacity to validate p95 under your production-like traffic. We'll instrument metrics and run a diff-eval against your baseline."

Open questions we should answer before finalizing the deck:
- Define the canonical sample size and anonymization requirements for transcript uploads.
- Decide on a short default reserved pool sizing heuristic (e.g., 2x steady qps for headroom).
- Create a templated diff-eval report format for SEs to hand to customers.

Quick assets to attach to this doc (links to be populated by SEs):
- capacity-template.csv (sheet)
- dedicated-provision-playbook.md (confluence)
- diff-eval-template.xlsx

Next actions (owner + due dates):
- Marcus: populate capacity-template.csv with retail example by 2025-03-05.
- Jordan: draft the 6-slide micro-deck and upload to Drive by 2025-03-07.
- Alyssa (owner): run one internal spike with synthetic retail workload and attach results by 2025-03-12.

Notes to self (scratch):
- Avoid heavy legal language on early calls; use "data residency" not "data sovereignty" until legal is involved.
- Keep quantization talk high-level with customers; offer to run measurements rather than debate theory live.

End of microcards v1 — iterate after two real POCs to capture new objections and sample numbers.
